fichas.title: One flat per floor (town villa)
fichas.summary: Identical or similar flats are stacked on multiple storeys and reached by a common stairway. One flat is accessed on each floor. This arrangement uses a relatively high proportion of floor area for access, but may provide the feeling of a stacked terrace. The text gives a general limitation of four floors without a lift.
uses: Vertical access to one dwelling per floor

fichas.title: Two flats per floor
fichas.summary: Two flats per floor is described as the most common vertical-access arrangement, balancing residential quality and value for money. It supports varied and flexible floor-plan solutions and adaptation to different compass orientations.

fichas.title: Three flats per floor
fichas.summary: Three flats per floor are presented as a favourable combination of residential quality and value for money, and as suitable for corner buildings. Flats with differing numbers of rooms can be arranged on the same floor. The diagrams show one-flight stair and corner solutions.
uses: Vertical access to three flats per floor
Arranging flats with different room counts on one floor

fichas.title: Four flats per floor and point houses
fichas.summary: Four flats per floor can provide an adequate balance of residential quality and value for money when floor plans are designed appropriately. Point houses allow differentiated orientation of flats on each floor. Lifts are required in residential buildings of more than five full floors; buildings more than 22 m above ground level are subject to high-rise provisions.
uses: Vertical access to four flats per floor
